title: Blood Plasma Coenzyme Q10 and P-Selectin Are Predictive Factors for Mild Cognitive Dysfunction in Elderly Women
content: Detection of the early phases of cognitive dysfunction is critical for identifying individuals at risk of neurodegeneration before irreversible damage occurs. High levels of Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) in plasma are associated with high cognitive and executive capacities. Maintenance of endothelial function is also an important factor in the prevention of neurodegeneration and dementia. Therefore, this study aimed to determine plasma markers of endothelial health that, in conjunction with CoQ10, can effectively serve as predictors of cognitive dysfunction in a cohort of 45 elderly women (78.36 ± 8.41 years) from Seville, Spain. Utilizing a cross-sectional design, we assessed cognitive and executive capacities via the widely used MMSE-30 and FAB-E scales. Physiological health was evaluated through plasma biomarkers (including GDF-15, GFAP, BDNF, P-selectin, NfL, and p-Tau181) and the determination of CoQ10 levels. Furthermore, the study also analyzed exosome levels by measuring CD63, and their content in DNA and mtDNA. Our results indicate that low plasma CoQ10, elevated P-selectin (P-sel), and reduced exosomal DNA content can serve as early warning signs of neurodegeneration, appearing before traditional markers like GFAP, NfL, or p-Tau181. Our results indicate a link between CoQ10 levels, endothelial damage, and cognitive dysfunction risk.
